title: Flock Credibility Lost as It Repeatedly Lies to City Councils, Police, & Public
why: If your city runs Flock ALPR cameras, the vendor's own statements about heat maps, federal access, and abuse controls have been documented as false, so the surveillance surface is wider than officials were told.
notes: Oshkosh, WI set a record: the council revoked its Flock contract one day after approving it, after Flock's CISO told members the system did not 'create a pattern or heat map of an individual's movement.' Flock later admitted the system produces a heat map of where a vehicle's images were captured for up to a month, and dismissed the false statement as 'one small misconception' and 'a minor nuance.'

In Loveland, CO, Flock told the police chief and press it had no federal contracts, then admitted it held pilot contracts with CBP and DHS giving those agencies direct access to license-plate data; the CEO said Flock 'inadvertently provided inaccurate information.'

Flock published a blog titled 'Does Flock Share Data With ICE? No,' asserting ICE lacks direct access, while ICE and CBP obtained indirect access through state and local police customers; the CEO later conceded Flock was used for immigration enforcement but called it not Flock's problem.

Texas law enforcement reportedly used Flock ALPR data in May 2025 to track someone seeking abortion care in Illinois. Flock's response, a 'Proactive Search Term Tool,' failed in ACLU of Massachusetts audits: one Oregon department entered 'investigation' 111 times and 'hehehe' 20 times in the search-reason field in September 2025 alone, bypassing trigger words like 'abortion.'

Flock's public-affairs staff claimed on social media it partnered with the ACLU of New Mexico to craft ALPR legislation, and told Urbana, IL councilmembers in 2021 it 'worked with groups like the ACLU'; the ACLU says neither it nor any affiliate has ever partnered with Flock.

The piece is an ACLU advocacy post, not a neutral audit; it frames the pattern as deliberate lying and urges governments to refuse Flock and, if using ALPRs at all, to limit data retention, data sharing, and enforcement scope.
summary: The ACLU documents a pattern of Flock Safety, a major supplier of automatic license plate readers to police, misrepresenting its surveillance capabilities and data-sharing practices to city councils, police departments, and the public. Cited examples include Oshkosh, WI, where the council revoked a Flock contract one day after approval because Flock's CISO falsely denied the system builds vehicle heat maps (which Flock later admitted retain up to a month); Loveland, CO, where Flock denied federal contracts before admitting CBP and DHS pilot access; and a blog denying ICE data sharing while ICE had indirect access through local-police customers. The article also says Texas police used Flock data to track a person seeking abortion care in Illinois, and that Flock's remediation tool failed because officers enter vague search reasons like 'investigation' or 'hehehe.' It further alleges Flock falsely claimed to have partnered with the ACLU on system design and legislation. The post is explicit advocacy: it argues officials should distrust Flock's claims and, if they use ALPRs at all, impose strict limits on retention, sharing, and enforcement uses.
novelty: documented pattern of ALPR vendor misrepresenting surveillance capabilities to officials
audience: engineers/policymakers tracking surveillance tech, privacy law, and public-sector vendor accountability

title: Linux kernel will support $ORIGIN, sort of
why: A programmable binfmt_misc hook headed for -next lets the kernel rewrite PT_INTERP at exec time, which is the missing piece for building relocatable Nix, Bazel, and Buck binaries that find their loader via $ORIGIN instead of a hardcoded /nix/store path.
notes: The author (Farid Zakaria) first proposed direct $ORIGIN support in the VFS layer on the LKML; VFS maintainer Christian Brauner instead steered it toward eBPF struct_ops attached to binfmt_misc, so the interpreter is chosen by a verified in-kernel program rather than a fixed rule.

The sample handler uses two BPF_PROG hooks: a match that checks the ELF magic bytes (bpf_strncmp on the first 4 bytes), and a load that reads the binary's path via bpf_path_d_path and calls bpf_binprm_set_interp to derive the loader location; registration is via bpftool struct_ops register plus an echo to /proc/sys/fs/binfmt_misc/register.

Traditional binfmt_misc hijacks process identity: the registered interpreter becomes the process, so argv[0], /proc/<pid>/cmdline, and /proc/self/exe report the interpreter, not the binary you ran, which breaks programs that self-locate via /proc/self/exe.

Brauner's follow-up patch series adds new dispatch modes including a loader-substitution 'L' flag: the matched binary runs natively as the main image and only the PT_INTERP loader is swapped, so a stock ld.so works unchanged and identity leaks disappear.

Plan is to gate the handler on a new PT_INTERP_NIX segment rather than matching every ELF, keeping existing Nix binaries working and letting only opt-in binaries become relocatable; the author intends to upstream a NixOS module once the series ships in a tagged release.
Status is forward-looking: the patch series is described as heading into -next, not yet in a tagged kernel; claims about behavior come from the author's own account of the mailing-list collaboration.
summary: A blog post recounts a Nix contributor's attempt to make binaries relocatable by getting the Linux kernel to resolve $ORIGIN in PT_INTERP and shebangs. His initial LKML proposal to patch the VFS was redirected by maintainer Christian Brauner toward an eBPF-based approach: a struct_ops program registered with binfmt_misc that programmatically selects a binary's interpreter at exec time. A sample handler matches ELF magic bytes and derives the loader path from the binary's own location, giving $ORIGIN-style behavior. Because classic binfmt_misc makes the interpreter own the process identity (breaking argv[0], /proc/self/exe, and cmdline), Brauner added new dispatch modes, notably a loader-substitution 'L' flag that runs the matched binary as the main image and only overrides its PT_INTERP loader. The author plans to gate matching on a new PT_INTERP_NIX segment for backward compatibility and upstream a NixOS module once the patches land in -next and ship in a release. The mechanics and status are the author's self-reported account of an in-progress patch series.
novelty: eBPF-programmable binfmt_misc lets kernel pick interpreter dynamically, enabling $ORIGIN support
audience: Linux kernel/systems engineers, Nix/Bazel/Buck build-system maintainers

title: 7 Sandbox Escape Vulnerabilities Across 4 Coding Agent Vendors
why: If you run Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, or Antigravity on a dev box, the sandbox does not contain the agent's blast radius: it can write config that an unsandboxed helper on the same machine executes microseconds later, reaching your SSH keys, cloud tokens, and release paths.
notes: Pillar Research reports reproducing 7 sandbox escapes across 4 vendors (Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, Antigravity); these are vendor-attributed self-reported findings released as a daily 'Week of Sandbox Escapes' series, with no CVEs or vendor responses cited in the text.

The unifying mechanism: the agent rarely breaks the sandbox directly, it writes a file inside the workspace that a trusted host component later runs, loads, or scans (Python interpreter discovery, Git integrations, VSCode task runners, hook engines, the Docker Desktop socket).

Four failure modes named: (1) denylist sandboxes that can't enumerate every dangerous OS operation (Antigravity Seatbelt profile), (2) workspace config that is really executable code (.vscode Secure Mode bypass, hooks, virtualenv interpreters, git config, fsmonitor helpers), (3) allowlists that trust command names not invocations (Codex allowed 'git show', but git flags can write files, load config, run hooks), (4) privileged local daemons outside the box (Docker socket gives host reach the agent lacks).

Stated threat-model shift: sandbox boundaries have three layers, direct execution, workspace writes, and host trust; the escapes live in the third, so blocking filesystem writes while leaving a daemon API open just moves the boundary to that API.

Pillar frames this as marketing for its own endpoint product, which instruments the 'seam', provenance on what the agent wrote plus a record when an unsandboxed component reads and executes it, rather than watching the agent process or filenames.

Buyer checklist offered: ask what the agent can write, which host components trust those writes, which local daemons it reaches, which commands skip approval, whether policy is enforced on names/paths or actual side effects, and whether the tool can distinguish user-created from agent-created project state.
summary: Pillar Research says it found and reproduced seven sandbox escapes across four AI coding agents, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, and Antigravity, arguing that agentic tools have become endpoint infrastructure without being governed as such. In nearly every case the agent did not break its sandbox directly; instead it wrote a file it was permitted to write, which a trusted, unsandboxed host component later executed, loaded, or scanned. The findings cluster into four failure modes: denylist sandboxes that cannot keep up with OS complexity (Antigravity's Seatbelt profile), workspace configuration that is effectively executable code (.vscode Secure Mode bypass, hooks, virtualenvs, git config, fsmonitor helpers), allowlists that trust command names rather than exact invocations (Codex's 'git show', where flags can write files or run hooks), and privileged local daemons like the Docker socket that give host reach the agent itself lacks. The core claim is that an agent's blast radius is not the agent process but everything it can write that the host later trusts, so sandboxing the process alone leaves the trust handoff unmonitored. The piece doubles as promotion for Pillar's endpoint product, which instruments that seam via provenance and execution records; findings are self-reported and the text cites no CVEs or vendor responses.
novelty: host-trust escapes, not sandbox process breakouts
audience: security engineers and devtool builders adopting AI coding agents

title: An ordinary laptop solved a problem thought to require a quantum computer
why: The D-Wave dynamics simulation that a March 2025 Science paper called beyond classical reach now runs on a laptop, moving the classical-quantum frontier and raising the bar for what counts as quantum advantage.
notes: Team: Simons Foundation Flatiron Institute CCQ (Joseph Tindall, first author; Miles Stoudenmire) with Boston University collaborators, published in Science 2026 (vol 392, p868, DOI 10.1126/science.adx2728).

Target: dynamics of hundreds of interacting qubits on square, cubic, and diamond lattices, the same class of problem King et al. (many D-Wave authors) argued in a March 2025 Science paper could not be matched classically (DOI 10.1126/science.ado6285).

Method: tensor networks compress the exponentially large wave function (Tindall's analogy: a zip file of interconnected small number tables), run via CCQ's ITensor library; 3D dynamics modeled with a 3D tensor network the authors call an untrodden frontier and a software-engineering challenge.

Belief propagation, a 1980s algorithm recently adapted to quantum systems, handled early calculations: more approximate but far cheaper, letting it start on 3D problems older exact methods could not attempt.
Reported results: matched theoretical predictions, agreed with the earlier quantum-computer simulations, and were checkable on smaller instances; all claims are self-reported by the CCQ team.
Next target: systems with electrons hopping between sites, described as quantitatively harder and closer to real quantum materials like superconductors.
summary: Researchers at the Simons Foundation's Flatiron Institute (CCQ) and Boston University report in Science (2026) that they simulated the dynamics of hundreds of entangled qubits on square, cubic, and diamond lattices using tensor networks, with some calculations run on a personal laptop. The problem was chosen deliberately because a March 2025 Science paper (King et al., largely D-Wave authors) had used a quantum computer for this class of dynamics and argued classical machines could not match it. The CCQ team compressed the exponentially large wave function with tensor networks via their ITensor library, and used belief propagation, a cheaper if more approximate 1980s algorithm recently adapted to quantum systems, to reach 3D problems that older exact methods could not start. They say results matched theoretical predictions, checked out on smaller solvable instances, and agreed with the prior quantum-computer results without quantum hardware. The authors frame classical and quantum simulation as synergistic rather than purely competitive, and name electron-hopping systems relevant to real materials as their harder next goal. All accuracy claims are self-reported.
novelty: 3D tensor networks + belief propagation beat claimed quantum-only simulation
audience: quantum computing researchers and skeptics of quantum advantage claims

title: Understanding Reasoning from Pretraining to Post-Training
why: If you budget RL post-training, this argues you can predict post-RL reasoning performance from pretraining loss before spending any RL compute, and that longer pretraining raises the ceiling RL can reach.
notes: Uses chess as a controlled testbed: pretrain LMs from 5M to 1B params on human games, SFT on synthetic reasoning traces, then RL on puzzles with verifiable rewards, isolating pretraining vs RL contributions.
Claimed scaling result: post-RL performance at a fixed RL compute level is well-predicted by pretraining loss, and the slope of the RL reward curve improves roughly linearly with pretraining tokens.

Mechanism claim: RL does more than sharpen the SFT policy. On easy puzzles it amplifies correct moves SFT already preferred; on hard puzzles it surfaces correct moves that were nearly absent under SFT.
Transfer test: a 1B model pretrained on math-domain text shows the same pattern, with longer-pretrained checkpoints reaching higher post-RL performance and improving faster under RL.
Caveat: findings come from a narrow, verifiable-reward domain (chess plus one math replication) at small scale; no external benchmark or human-corpus generalization is demonstrated in the abstract.
summary: The paper studies how pretraining choices shape returns to reinforcement learning post-training, using chess as a controlled testbed for reasoning across the full pipeline. The authors pretrain language models from 5M to 1B parameters on human chess games, apply supervised fine-tuning on synthetic reasoning traces, then run RL on puzzles with verifiable rewards. They report that post-RL performance at a given RL compute level is well-predicted by pretraining loss, and that the slope of RL reward curves scales approximately linearly with pretraining tokens. They also characterize what RL does: on easy puzzles it amplifies moves the SFT policy already favored, while on hard puzzles it surfaces correct moves nearly absent under SFT. A 1B model pretrained on math-domain text reproduces the predictive pattern, which the authors offer as evidence the results extend beyond chess.
novelty: controlled chess testbed links pretraining scale to RL reasoning gains
audience: ML researchers studying RL post-training and reasoning scaling laws

title: Meta Garbage Collection: Using OCaml's GC to GC Rust
why: A verification tool cut a common quadratic blowup to linear in about 40 lines by making OCaml's garbage collector reclaim Tree Borrows state, turning a 3.02s run into 0.54s.
notes: Soteria Rust is an OCaml symbolic-execution tool that checks Rust programs against Tree Borrows, tracking every reference to a memory location as a tree of five-state nodes; each read/write updates node states, and reaching the fault state signals UB.

The slowdown came from unoptimized MIR: the tool cannot enable compiler optimizations (inlining, dead-code elimination) because they can erase the UB it hunts, so Range::next reborrows persist. Each Iterator::next call adds 9 nodes and ~10 accesses per iteration, giving 9N+10 nodes and 10N+12 accesses (9,010 nodes, 10,012 accesses at N=1000), roughly 45N-squared node accesses.

Soundness argument for dropping nodes: UB is only reachable via a local access, a finished loop iteration's branch has no live references, protected nodes (on function entry) are kept alive by the interpreter, children are always at least as close to UB as parents, and pre-branch state references prevent cross-branch collection in symbolic execution.

Implementation stores the tree as a weak map plus Weak sets and Ephemeron so nodes are held strongly only where their Rust reference is live; a node keeps all ancestors directly, so GCing an intermediate node preserves local/foreign relationships.

OCaml's periodic GC initially ran too rarely (low allocation) and left only the weak-reference cost, so they force Gc.major() when tree size exceeds threshold T, with backoff doubling T to 2T when a run frees nothing; T=256 gave the best balance, 0.54s at N=1000 (5.6x) and 10.6x at N=2000.

On a Tokio init snippet scaled from 64 to 1024, time dropped from 14.8s to 1.7s (8.7x, self-reported); a comparable unnamed tool that does not track Tree Borrows took 15.4s. Some benchmarks got slower from weak-reference overhead. Miri already GCs these trees but must implement it manually since its host language is Rust.
summary: Soteria Rust, an OCaml-based symbolic execution tool that verifies Rust against the Tree Borrows aliasing model, hit quadratic runtime on a simple increment loop because unoptimized MIR generates repeated reborrows (from Iterator::next desugaring) that grow the per-location reference tree by about 9 nodes and 10 accesses per iteration. At N=1000 the tree reached 9,010 nodes and 10,012 accesses, with 87% of the 3.02s runtime inside Tree Borrows. The fix, roughly 40 lines, holds tree nodes weakly using OCaml's Weak sets and Ephemeron and lets OCaml's garbage collector reclaim nodes from finished iterations, justified because UB is only reachable via local accesses on live references. Because OCaml's GC runs too rarely under low allocation, the authors force major collections when the tree exceeds a threshold T (best at 256) with a 2T backoff when nothing is freed. This restored linear time with up to a claimed 10.6x speedup, and cut a scaled Tokio init benchmark from 14.8s to 1.7s, though some benchmarks slowed due to weak-reference overhead. The authors frame this as reusing the host language's GC, contrasting with Miri, which must implement tree GC manually because its host language is Rust.
novelty: delegating symbolic-exec state cleanup to host language's GC
audience: systems/PL engineers building verification tools and interpreters

title: How we measured AI writing across arXiv, and where the measurement breaks
why: Roughly a third of new arXiv papers, and about 65% in computer science, now read as machine-written by a detector calibrated so that pre-ChatGPT text flags at only 0.4%, which sets a defensible floor under the usual "N% is now AI" headline.
notes: Method: 12,750 papers scored across ten field groups, ~25 papers/field/month from Jan 2023 to Jul 2026, plus eight control months in 2021-2022; version-1 PDFs only, so 2026 revisions cannot leak modern text into 2023 slots.

Calibration anchor: the threshold is set so exactly 0.4% of pre-ChatGPT (2021-2022) papers trip it; at that rate the detector self-reports clearing 99.6% of genuine pre-LLM text and recovering 85% of AI academic text.

Trend: flagged share flat at 0.4% through 2021-2022, lifts within months of ChatGPT, reaches ~32% over the most recent complete quarter and peaks near 39% in early 2026; every figure carries a bootstrap 95% CI.

Field spread: computer science ~65% [59.3, 70.3] highest, mathematics ~0.7% [0.0, 1.7] lowest; the authors say full body text is scored because abstracts understate the signal (one paper scored under 20% on abstract, over 70% on body).

Stated limitations: each per-field control is only 200 papers (about eight total flags across the 2,000-paper control), so per-field control rates are approximate; math's low score may be detector blind spot since sparse prose is out-of-distribution, not proof of low adoption.

Framing caveats: incomplete generator coverage means the reported prevalence is a lower bound, and a flag estimates 'reads as machine-written' (including heavy AI-assisted editing), not authorship; the authors say the tool is free and they make no money from it.
summary: The authors scored the full body text of 12,750 arXiv papers with an academic-writing detector calibrated so that pre-ChatGPT (2021-2022) papers flag at a 0.4% false-positive rate, using those years as a built-in control against detector artifacts. They report the flagged share is flat at 0.4% before 2023, rises within months of ChatGPT, and reaches about 32% over the most recent complete quarter, peaking near 39% in early 2026. Field variation is wide: computer science flags at about 65% while mathematics sits near 0.7%, and the authors argue math's low value may reflect the detector being out-of-distribution for notation-heavy, prose-sparse papers rather than genuinely low adoption. They frame the numbers as lower bounds because generator coverage is incomplete, and note per-field controls rest on only 200 papers each (roughly eight flags total across the control set). They stress a flag means text reads as machine-written, including heavy AI-assisted editing, and is not evidence of authorship by any specific person; the detector is offered free.
novelty: calibrated arXiv-wide AI-writing detector with pre-LLM false-positive floor
audience: researchers and engineers tracking AI's impact on scientific publishing/authorship

title: You only need the frontier model for one single edit
why: If an agent's bill is dominated by reads, the standard plan-then-cheap-execute split doubles the expensive part; the article's own benchmarks put frontier-quality work at roughly half the cost by handing off the live context window instead of a plan document.
notes: The core claim: an agent's cost scales as O(reads), not compute. In one anecdotal trace ~9% of tokens were edits and the rest was reading, so a plan handoff makes both models read everything (once at frontier prices, once at cheap prices) rather than moving the expensive part.

/plan is shown to lose: Opus-plans-read-only + Gemini-Flash-executes lands at $3.18/12.7min/84.6% pass, while Opus doing the whole task solo is $2.78/10.1min at the same 84.6% pass, i.e. the 'saving' costs 14% more.

/prewalk mechanism: start on the frontier model with a hidden 'plan deeply, capture as a todo list, then start' instruction; the moment the first edit lands, swap to the cheap model and prune the planning instruction from context, so the cheap model inherits exploration plus one valid in-context edit and never sees a planning frame.

Self-reported benchmarks. GPT-5.6: /prewalk 85% / $1.04 / 300s vs oneshot Luna executor 77% / $0.60 / 570s and frontier Sol oneshot 88% / $1.71 / 372s. Opus 4.8: /prewalk 78% / $1.46 / 402s vs Gemini Flash 3.5 oneshot 60% / $1.16 / 360s and Opus oneshot 85% / $2.78 / 606s.

Reliability came from the todo list, not the edit trigger: swapping at a fixed turn or on first edit alone failed (small models declared tasks done early); a validation-gated todo list with an item cap kept the cheap model steered. Reported side effect: /prewalk traces showed no web-search 'cheating' for known GitHub fixes while /plan did, attributed (as the authors' 'best explanation') to cutting the frontier model off ~7-turn median before its googling phase.

Framed as a prefill descendant: prefilling assistant turns (once a jailbreak class, now blocked at inference nearly everywhere, per the author since Anthropic's Sonnet 4.5) is replaced by handing the model innocuous already-happened turns. Shipped in the open-source omp harness as --prewalk / --prewalk-into <model> / /prewalk.
summary: The piece argues that agent cost is dominated by reading, not editing or thinking (roughly 9% of tokens are edits in a sample trace), so the popular pattern of using a frontier model to write a plan and a cheap model to execute it duplicates the expensive read work: the plan document is a ~2K-token 'postcard' that discards the 100K+ tokens of grounded context, forcing the executor to re-read files. Benchmarks in the post show plan-handoff (Opus plans, Flash executes) costing more than Opus solo at identical pass rates. The authors propose /prewalk: run the frontier model with a hidden plan-then-act instruction, let it explore and land the first edit, then swap to a cheap model while pruning the planning instruction, so the cheap model inherits the actual context window plus a valid in-context example. Self-reported results claim ~92-97% of frontier pass rate at ~53-61% of cost and higher speed for both GPT-5.6 and Opus 4.8 configurations, and note prewalk traces did not resort to web-search 'cheating' the way plan runs did. Robustness relied on gating the model swap on a validation-checked todo list rather than a fixed turn count or a bare first edit. The technique is framed as a benign application of prefill/autoregression and ships in the open-source omp harness. All numbers are the authors' own; benchmark methodology beyond task examples like django-13279 is not fully detailed.
novelty: context handoff beats plan-doc handoff for cheap-model execution
audience: engineers building multi-model agent pipelines/coding harnesses

title: Five US tech giants' hidden debts soar to $1.65tn on opaque AI funding
why: The AI buildout is being financed through obligations that don't show up as debt on balance sheets, so the risk you're pricing into these five stocks understates their real leverage by an estimated $1.65tn.
notes: Nikkei estimates off-balance-sheet debt across five US tech giants at $1.65tn, up roughly eightfold in about four years; the figure now exceeds these companies' reported on-balance-sheet debt.
Meta alone carries about $420bn in off-balance-sheet debt, nearly triple its transparent debt, per the study.
The mechanisms cited are data center leases and GPU supply contracts, arrangements that create liabilities without appearing as conventional borrowing.
Meta and Oracle are named among the five companies studied; the article excerpt does not identify the other three.
This is a Nikkei study, not audited disclosure; the $1.65tn is an estimate, and the excerpt does not detail the methodology behind it.
The stated stake: opaque funding makes it harder for investors to assess risk as AI capital spending balloons.
summary: A Nikkei study estimates that off-balance-sheet, or "hidden," debt across five US tech giants has reached about $1.65tn, up roughly eightfold in four years as AI investment surged. The study says this hidden debt now exceeds the companies' transparent, on-balance-sheet debt, complicating investors' ability to gauge risk. The liabilities stem from arrangements such as data center leases and GPU supply contracts rather than conventional borrowing. Meta is highlighted with roughly $420bn in off-balance-sheet debt, nearly triple its reported debt. Meta and Oracle are named among the five firms; the excerpt does not list the others or the estimate's methodology. The figures are Nikkei's own estimates rather than audited disclosures.
novelty: off-balance-sheet AI debt hit $1.65tn, up 8x in 4 years
audience: investors and engineers tracking AI infrastructure financing risk

title: China’s open-weights AI strategy is winning
why: If a16z's cited 80% figure holds, the open Chinese models most startups already depend on are commoditizing the exact layer OpenAI and Anthropic charge for, putting the AI-driven portion of US spending at risk.
notes: Core argument: model weights themselves carry little moat because API access makes swapping vendors trivial; the durable moat sits in enterprise services, integrations, and contracts around the model.

Strategy claim: US GPU export controls block Chinese firms from running OpenAI/Anthropic-style centralized global services, so releasing weights openly turns a compute disadvantage into a permissionless distribution advantage that commoditizes the paid layer.

Cited numbers stay claims: Martin Casado (a16z), via the Economist, estimates an 80% chance any given startup uses Chinese models; Moonshot and Alibaba released models they claim rival OpenAI and Anthropic at a fraction of the cost. No benchmark methodology is given.
Author's caveat: open weights are not open source but are portable and permissionless, and these models still carry Chinese government content restrictions (example given: Tiananmen Square).

Forward claim, presented as opinion: the author expects AI spending to fall and warns the outcome could be severe given how much of the US economy runs on it; he backs 'public AI,' federated services, and open research but says US incentives push labs toward first-order profit instead.
summary: The essay argues that AI models have little standing moat beyond brand and switching friction, since API access lets users swap ChatGPT for Claude or a Chinese model with minimal workflow change. Because US GPU export controls stop Chinese firms from offering centralized global cloud services, the author frames China's open-weights releases as a deliberate strategy: commoditize the layer where US labs make money and win the infrastructure ecosystem through permissionless distribution. He cites the Economist reporting that Moonshot and Alibaba released models they claim match OpenAI and Anthropic at lower cost, and a16z's Martin Casado estimating an 80% chance a given startup uses Chinese models. He notes these open models still reflect Chinese government content restrictions, using Tiananmen Square as an example. The piece closes by predicting a drop in AI spending and calling for US backing of public AI, federated services, and open research to realign incentives.
novelty: argues open-weights is deliberate Chinese strategic response to US export controls

title: Hacker wipes Romania's land registry database
why: A single attacker with valid credentials halted Romania's entire real-estate market for a week and forced a national agency to rebuild its network from scratch, a reminder that destructive extortion against public registries is now a repeat pattern, not a one-off.
notes: Per Risky Business sources, the hacker logged into Romania's ANCPI cadastre agency with valid credentials, mapped internal systems, then wiped systems and backups after failing to extort the agency; data deletion began July 14, and stolen data (employee credentials, internal documents, network details) went up for sale on a hacking forum a day later.

The agency appears to have kept an offline backup that survived the wipe; officials restored the website and announced they are rebuilding the entire network from scratch. Notaries could not record transactions and citizens could not obtain proof of ownership while apps, sites, and email were down.

The attacker posts as ByteToBreach; KELA's December profile placed them in Algeria and, after this hack, updated the post to name Zakaria Mahdjoub of Oran, Algeria. Same actor is tied to a breach of Sweden's e-government portal this year.
Romania becomes at least the sixth country in three years to have its land registry agency hacked, joining Poland, Slovakia, Greece, Morocco, Russia, and Ukraine.

In a separate bulletin item, Hugging Face says an autonomous AI agent breached it via its data-processing pipeline, stealing internal datasets and some cloud credentials (no customer data, per the company); Hugging Face's own frontier-model guardrails blocked using the model for incident response because they could not distinguish an IR event from offensive operations, forcing a switch to local models.
Attribution and identity claims come from KELA and Risky Business sources; no independent confirmation or arrest is reported, and the extortion-then-wipe narrative is sourced to unnamed parties.
summary: A hacker breached Romania's National Agency for Cadastre and Real Estate Advertising (ANCPI) using valid credentials, mapped internal systems, and wiped both systems and backups after a failed extortion attempt, according to Risky Business sources. The wipe, which began July 14, took the country's land registry offline for a week, stalling property transactions and blocking citizens from obtaining ownership records; stolen employee credentials, internal documents, and network details were listed for sale on a hacking forum the next day. An offline backup appears to have survived, and the agency is rebuilding its network from scratch. The account behind the leak, ByteToBreach, was profiled by KELA and named as Zakaria Mahdjoub of Oran, Algeria, and is also linked to a breach of Sweden's e-government portal this year. Romania is at least the sixth country in three years to have its land registry hacked. The same Risky Business bulletin separately reports that Hugging Face was breached by an autonomous AI agent exploiting its data-processing pipeline, and that Hugging Face's own model guardrails blocked using a frontier model for incident response.
novelty: nation-state land registry wiped after failed extortion, not just breached

title: Using ThinkPad T480 as a mobile phone
why: A stock ThinkPad T480, freed by Libreboot, can place and receive real cellular calls, showing that a fully user-controlled, free-software phone is buildable from a laptop and one modem card.
notes: A bug in Intel Management Engine lets the author flash Libreboot over stock firmware, which drops the WWAN card whitelist and allows an arbitrary modem in the SIM/LTE slot.
The modem is a Quectel EG25-G, the same part used in the PinePhone; it runs an ARM core with Android internally, and a community firmware exposes a free-software userspace.
The T480's PCM audio pins for the modem are not wired, so the custom firmware registers the modem as a USB audio interface to carry call audio; SMS and mobile data work without modification.
M.2 versions of the EG25-G are rare and ship without compatible antenna connectors, requiring finicky conversion cables the author describes as hard to work with.
Android apps run natively via Waydroid, so the setup is pitched as a full phone replacement rather than a demo.
Evidence is limited to a self-shot video of an incoming call plus a prose writeup; no benchmarks, call-quality measurements, or battery/portability tradeoffs are given.
summary: A blogger converts a Lenovo ThinkPad T480 into a working mobile phone that supports calls, SMS, and mobile data. Using an Intel Management Engine bug, they flash Libreboot to remove the WWAN card whitelist, then install a Quectel EG25-G modem, the same modem used in the PinePhone, which runs Android on an internal ARM core and has a free-software firmware available. Because the T480 does not wire the modem's PCM audio pins, the custom firmware registers the modem as a USB audio interface to route call audio; SMS and data work out of the box. The hardest part was sourcing a rare M.2 version of the EG25-G and fitting finicky antenna conversion cables. The author suggests the laptop can replace a phone entirely, with Android apps running via Waydroid, and shows an incoming call in a video.

title: How AST-grep Rewrote Tree-sitter in Rust and Made It 30% Faster
why: A single maintainer used ChatGPT to translate Tree-sitter's mature C parser into Rust and get 22% less user CPU end-to-end, evidence that agent-driven rewrites of load-bearing infrastructure are now cheap enough for one person to finish.
notes: Reported gains: +29.74% raw-parsing throughput and −22.2% user CPU on the ast-grep outline run (1.233s to 0.960s), self-measured on the opencode TypeScript repo; the '30%' in the title is parser-only, the 22% is end-to-end.

Memory is the tradeoff: the outline run's peak RSS rose from 26.52 MiB (C) to 34.43 MiB (Rust); on a TypeScript-compiler stress corpus, peak fell from 1.04 GiB in an earlier arena design to 91.2 MiB after several rounds of arena surgery.

This is a narrower runtime, not a drop-in Tree-sitter: incremental old-tree reuse and native loading of Wasm-compiled grammars were removed, because the target workload (AI agents parsing whole file snapshots) always reparses fresh; existing generated grammars and external scanners still work without regeneration.

Parser wins came from four principles: don't build the GLR graph-structured stack until input actually forks (about 99% of the observed stack was one straight path), use an arena instead of per-node allocations, precompute repeated grammar lookups, and give ASCII/single-action cases a short path.

A faster parser initially made ast-grep slower: the first arena reserved a huge virtual-memory region per parser, and across thousands of files the reserve/release syscalls and page-fault churn were the CPU regression; the fix was an ordinary small allocation that grows on demand.

Compatibility still requires many raw pointers and unsafe blocks; ABI-facing types and exported functions stay C-shaped. The work is AI-assisted (ChatGPT wrote the code, profiling, and instrumentation under the maintainer's direction), following similar rewrite attempts on Bun, pgrust, and Roc. All numbers are self-reported; this is part 1 of 4.
summary: ast-grep maintainer HerringtonDarkholme used ChatGPT to rewrite Tree-sitter's C parsing core in Rust, reporting +29.74% raw-parsing throughput and a 22.2% drop in end-to-end user CPU (1.233s to 0.960s) on the ast-grep outline workload, at the cost of higher peak memory (26.52 to 34.43 MiB). The result is a narrower runtime aimed at AI coding agents that parse complete file snapshots: it drops incremental old-tree reuse and native Wasm grammar loading while keeping the existing generated-grammar ecosystem working, and still relies on raw pointers and unsafe blocks for ABI compatibility. The process moved through a conservative parity-first translation (tests as oracle), a reverted 'vibe-coded' optimization that ran 20% faster but segfaulted, scope cuts, and readability refactors before real gains landed. Parser speedups came from deferring GLR graph construction until input forks (about 99% of observed stacks were linear), arena allocation, precomputed lookups, and short paths for common cases. A faster parser initially made ast-grep slower because a per-parser huge virtual-memory reservation caused syscall and page-fault churn across thousands of files; fixing that plus resolving old-tree stress-corpus memory (down from 1.04 GiB to 91.2 MiB) and reworking tree-reader lookups closed the regression. All figures are self-reported; the piece is part 1 of a four-part series.
novelty: AI-assisted C-to-Rust rewrite of Tree-sitter core, tuned for agent workloads
audience: devtools engineers building code-analysis/agentic coding tools on Tree-sitter

title: Everyone Should Know SIMD
why: Any hot loop scanning contiguous bytes, characters, or ints is a candidate for a 4x-16x speedup you can write yourself in about a dozen lines, without dropping to intrinsics or assembly.
notes: The reusable pattern is five steps: broadcast constants and init accumulators, loop one vector-width chunk at a time, do the parallel compare/arithmetic, reduce or store the result, then a scalar tail loop for the remainder and for CPUs with no supported vector width.

Worked example from Ghostty scans decoded codepoints for the first value at or below 0xF (a C0 control): a 1-line scalar while loop becomes ~12 lines using Zig builtins @Vector, @splat, values > threshold, @reduce(.And), @bitCast to an integer mask, and @ctz to locate the first failing lane.

Claimed per-lane speedups scale with vector width: up to 4x on ARM NEON (including Apple Silicon), 8x on AVX2, 16x on AVX-512 (Intel plus AMD Zen 4 and newer); author's measured end-to-end throughput was ~5x on an AVX2 Intel desktop, self-reported without published methodology.

Zig's generic @Vector removes CPU-specific syntax but not codegen: the compiler still lowers to the target's instruction set, and Ghostty's simd.lanes(u32) returns null to skip SIMD entirely on unsupported targets, using the same scalar loop as fallback and tail.

SIMD only pays off over hundreds to millions of contiguous bytes; a handful or dozens is not worth it. Author argues explicit SIMD is preferable to auto-vectorization, which he says compilers do poorly and can silently regress on unrelated changes.

Author flags that projects like simdutf and simdjson use far more complex techniques that are not the everyday case, and notes the post was hand-written with no AI assistance, adapted from a Lobsters comment.
summary: Mitchell Hashimoto argues that the common case of SIMD, processing N values per iteration instead of one, is a routine pattern most engineers should recognize rather than an exotic optimization. He lays out a five-step shape: broadcast constants, loop one vector-width chunk at a time, run the parallel operation, reduce or store the result, and finish with a scalar tail that also covers unsupported CPUs. A concrete Ghostty example vectorizes a scan for the first codepoint at or below 0xF, turning a one-line scalar loop into about twelve lines using Zig builtins (@Vector, @splat, @reduce, @bitCast, @ctz). Claimed speedups scale with lane width (up to 4x NEON, 8x AVX2, 16x AVX-512), with a self-reported ~5x measured end-to-end on an AVX2 desktop. He notes compilers can auto-vectorize simple loops but do it unreliably, so explicit SIMD is worth writing when a speedup matters. The payoff requires processing large, contiguous data; small inputs are not worth it.
novelty: demystifies SIMD as a routine 5-step pattern, not exotic optimization
audience: systems/application engineers who avoid SIMD due to perceived complexity

title: Maybe we should revisit microkernels
why: The classic reason microkernels lost — a context switch on every I/O syscall — is largely gone on hardware you already own, so the security and fault-isolation arguments are worth re-pricing.
notes: The thesis: microkernels put everything in userspace except scheduling, I/O device access, and IPC, buying per-driver fault isolation (a driver bug or crash stays contained instead of taking the whole system down).

Historical killer was overhead: 1980s machines had no way for userspace to touch hardware directly, so each filesystem disk read meant a syscall, a context switch, and expensive locking plus memory copying.

The claimed unlock is the IOMMU, standard on PCs for roughly a decade, which manages device access in hardware and lets userspace reach devices directly; combined with shared memory it can remove context switches from the happy path when enough cores are available.
Proposed zero-copy IPC: shared buffers plus atomic compare-and-swap used as a ring-buffer command queue for async, lockless, copy-free message passing — the same pattern GPU/DRM drivers already use.

Implementation sketch is all reuse, not new code: Xen as the hypervisor/scheduler layer, Mach-style servers copied from FreeBSD for network/filesystem, Linux's async-command-buffer graphics subsystem run in userspace; shared libraries linked at launch exokernel-style.

Stated caveat: Mach (ancestor of XNU in macOS/iOS) folded its userspace servers back into the kernel for performance until it was effectively monolithic — a cautionary precedent the piece acknowledges but argues IOMMU-era hardware changes.
summary: A blog post argues the case against microkernels — high overhead — was a product of 1980s hardware and is worth revisiting now. Its structure: microkernels move drivers and servers into userspace for better security, reliability, and modularity (it cites CrowdStrike and Linux driver-merging burden as examples of monolithic pain), but early microkernel OSes lost because every I/O required a syscall, context switch, locking, and copying. The author claims the IOMMU, standard on PCs for about a decade, plus shared-memory ring buffers using atomic compare-and-swap, can eliminate context switches on the happy path and give lockless, copy-free IPC — a pattern already common in GPU drivers. It sketches a buildable stack reusing Xen for hypervisor scheduling, FreeBSD/Mach-style servers, and Linux's DRM graphics subsystem in userspace, with shared libraries linked at launch exokernel-style. The piece is an opinion/design sketch, not an implementation or benchmark, and it self-flags the Mach precedent (servers reabsorbed into the kernel for performance) as the main counterexample.
novelty: IOMMU-era hardware could revive microkernels by killing context-switch overhead
audience: OS/systems engineers and kernel developers

title: Spatial languages: writing code in 2D
why: Reversible-computing patterns that read as unreadable back-and-forth gate lists in Qiskit become a two-line 2D expression, where the second row literally uncomputes the first.
notes: Core idea: expressions get a y-axis. A true 3-arity infix operator @@ (andFlip) takes two conditions above and a target below, toggling the target in place when both inputs are true; a single @ flips its target when one condition is true.
In-place toggle differs from `x and y and z`: @@ leaves a persistent result and a scratch bit (t1), so a modeled chicken-coop door moves once and stays rather than mirroring live sensor state.

Vertical chaining does ancilla uncomputation: stacking a second `(x @@ y) @@ z` / `(x @@ y)` row restores the borrowed intermediate t1 to its original unknown value n while still computing the correct t2. This maps to the CCCX gate and the Qiskit sequence ccx(x,y,t1); ccx(t1,z,t2); ccx(x,y,t1); ccx(t1,z,t2).

A rewrite operator := (shape on the left rewrites to expression on the right) defines new spatial operators: `maj` computes the majority of three inputs and `uma` (UnMajority-and-Add) cleans up, both taken from the classic quantum ripple-carry adder paper; three maj plus a uma row form a full 3-bit adder that resets its own scratch wires.
Prior art surveyed: Befunge (1993), Orca livecoding sequencer, Racket's shipping #2dcond, Hexagony, PLC ladder logic, and spreadsheets as the most-used 2D language.

Caveat: entirely conceptual. The author states an IDE and parser would need to cooperate but describes no working implementation, and the post ends on Sapir-Whorf and a David Foster Wallace nod rather than a tool.
summary: A blog post argues code should be writable in 2D rather than one-dimensional left-to-right text, using vertical layout to express true 3-arity infix operators. It defines toy operators @ (flip one target on one condition) and @@ (toggle a target below two conditions when both are true), which have Toffoli/CCX gate semantics, and uses a chicken-coop door controller as a concrete example of toggle-in-place versus `and`. The central demonstration is that stacking expression rows performs ancilla uncomputation: a second row restores a borrowed mutable intermediate t1 to its original unknown value while still producing the correct output, mirroring the CCCX gate and reproducing a four-instruction Qiskit CCX circuit that the author finds harder to follow. A rewrite operator := lets readers build higher-level spatial operators such as maj and uma from the quantum ripple-carry adder, composing into a self-cleaning 3-bit adder in one 2D expression. The piece closes with a tour of existing 2D languages (Befunge, Orca, Racket's #2dcond, Hexagony, ladder logic, spreadsheets). It is exploratory: no parser, IDE, or working implementation is provided.
novelty: 2D infix syntax mapping directly onto quantum circuit ancilla uncomputation
audience: language designers, PL researchers, and quantum computing enthusiasts curious about notation

title: Tencent WorkBuddy Bench: A Multi-Domain Coding-Agent Benchmark with Contamination-Resistant Task Construction
why: If you evaluate coding agents, this offers a fully open benchmark that resists training-data contamination without hiding the tasks, so you can re-run and audit every case yourself.
notes: Covers four work domains with separate verification styles: repository-level engineering (Code), front-end (Web), office and business workflows (Office), and red-/blue-team security (Security).

Contamination resistance comes from construction, not secrecy: each task is reverse-engineered from a real commit, pull request, or business scenario, then rewritten as a short colloquial role-played request so the prompt is not recoverable by web-searching the original issue or commit thread; it relies on dataset versioning too.
Full open release includes task directories, environment images, evaluation harness, tests, and reference solutions, making every task re-runnable and auditable by third parties.
Runs under a uniform, reproducible protocol on two agent harnesses, CodeBuddy Code and Claude Code, and reports a cross-model leaderboard across several model families.
Each subset uses a different scoring instrument, so scores are not comparable across subsets and no suite-wide average is reported.
From Tencent; the abstract documents methodology and leaderboard but does not include specific model scores or numeric results in the provided text.

The entire suite is released openly, including task directories, environment images, evaluation harness, tests, and reference solutions, so any third party can re-run and inspect each task.
